notes.b: A house is lived in for decades, so its design has to look good, work with the site and sun, and cause as little harm to the environment as possible. These factors shape the plan before any room is drawn.
points: Aesthetic factors: the elements of design (colour, pattern, shape, texture and line) and principles such as proportion, balance and harmony are used to create an attractive home that does not date quickly, so it stays pleasant and keeps its appeal.

Aspect (the direction a room faces): a south-facing living room gains the most daylight and solar heat, so living rooms go on the south side while bedrooms and utility rooms are placed according to their use and the sun's path.

Passive solar design uses the layout, orientation and glazing (glass areas) of the house to capture and retain heat without mechanical systems, which cuts heating costs because the sun does part of the work.

Environmental factors include using durable, sustainable and locally sourced materials, and minimising the energy used in making them and in running the house, so the home has a smaller impact over its life.
The house should fit its surroundings, with its scale and materials suiting the landscape and neighbouring buildings, so it does not look out of place.

Site slope and drainage affect the layout of the house, the foundations and the position of the garden, because a sloping or wet site needs different foundations and the water has to be drained away from the building.
notes.tip: Exams ask for factors that influence house design, so develop each factor with an example rather than just naming it: aesthetic and environmental factors sit alongside family needs and technology.

notes.b: A home must suit the people living in it now and the people they will become. Planning for both avoids costly alterations later.
points: The number and ages of family members determine the number of bedrooms, the bathrooms and the amount of living space, because a growing family needs more room than a couple.
Storage for clothing, sports and garden equipment must be provided in proportion to the size of the family, so that belongings do not clutter the living areas.
Teenagers need study space, and a home office may be needed where family members work from home, so a quiet room or corner is planned in.
Young children need safe design, such as a layout that allows supervision, so adults can see and reach them easily.
Room use should be planned so that each room suits its function, such as a utility room for washing and drying, which keeps laundry out of the kitchen.
Future needs are planned for by allowing space to extend, convert the attic or add a ground-floor bedroom, and by flexible rooms, for example a playroom that becomes a study as children grow.
Accessibility for ageing or for people with disabilities requires wide doors, level access and an accessible bathroom, so the home stays usable if someone's mobility changes.

To evaluate a house plan for a stated family, look at the relationship of kitchen, living and bedrooms, use of space, safety and supervision for children, storage, light and aspect, flexibility, accessibility and cost. Then name a strength, a weakness and a modification with a reason.
notes.tip: When asked to evaluate a plan for a stated family, give strengths such as kitchen position, space, garden access or a single storey for young children, then weaknesses, and two modifications for future needs, each with a reason tied to the family.

notes.h: Energy efficiency and the BER certificate
notes.b: A well-designed house keeps its heat in and uses fuel efficiently, which saves money and makes the home comfortable. The Building Energy Rating (BER) is the label that shows how well a home does this, much like the energy label on an appliance.
points: Insulation in the roof, walls (including cavity walls) or floor reduces heat loss, and double or triple glazing reduces heat loss through windows; draught proofing and a compact shape also cut the heat that escapes.
Heating systems can be made efficient with zoned heating (separate areas heated separately), thermostats and timers, or geothermal heating, so heat is supplied only where and when it is needed.
Renewable energy such as solar panels or a heat pump, efficient LED lighting and efficient appliances also cut fuel use, and passive solar gain heats the home for free.
A BER certificate rates a home's energy performance on a scale from A, the most efficient, to G, the least efficient. The very top band is now A0, a home that uses no fossil fuel for heating.

A registered BER assessor inspects the home and calculates the rating, measuring the area of the rooms and windows, the thickness of the walls, the levels of insulation, the heating system and the floor and wall types. The assessor then issues an advisory report on improvements.

A BER certificate is required by law when a home is built, sold or rented, and the rating must be shown in every advertisement for sale or rent, so buyers and tenants can compare running costs. It lasts ten years unless the home is upgraded.
Insulation, efficient heating and passive solar design all improve the BER rating and reduce running costs, and a better BER also means a more comfortable home and often a higher value.
notes.tip: For a BER question, cover the scale from A to G, that it is compulsory for homes built, sold or rented, that it is shown in advertisements, that a registered assessor does it, what the assessor measures, and the advice on improvements. For energy-saving features, give each feature with how it saves energy. Remember the BER is an energy rating, not a safety certificate or a structural warranty.

notes.b: Ergonomics means designing a space to suit the way people move and work in it, so everyday tasks are easy and safe. Technology adds ways to save energy and labour and to protect the home.
points: Ergonomics is the design of a space so that it suits how people move and work; in a kitchen, the sink, cooker and fridge are placed at the three points of an imaginary triangle (the work triangle), so the cook does not walk far between them.
Circulation space must allow people to move safely between work surfaces and to open doors and drawers without obstruction, because cramped layouts cause accidents.

Switches and sockets are placed at heights that can be reached comfortably, including by children and people with limited mobility, and counter heights and storage within easy reach follow the same idea. Stairs should be safe and the layout accessible.
Sensor lights and LED lamps reduce energy use in the home, because LEDs use little electricity and sensor lights switch on only when someone is there.

Zoned heating with programmers and smart thermostats, underfloor heating, solar thermal and solar photovoltaic panels, heat pumps and heat-recovery ventilation save energy, while centralised vacuum systems and smart home controls save labour.
Phone-linked alarm systems and electronic gates and garage doors add security to the home, because the owner can monitor and control access from anywhere.
Modern methods of construction, such as factory-built timber frame or panels, are a technological development in how the house itself is built.
notes.tip: Developments in technology are one of the three areas named in the design factors question, so give examples and say what each saves, whether energy, labour or security.

notes.b: The price of a house is more than the cost of building it. Costs fall into what you pay at the start and what you keep paying to maintain and run the home.
points: Initial costs include the site and servicing, the builder, materials, professional fees (architect, engineer), legal fees, planning and lender costs, mortgage costs, stamp duty on a purchase, and furnishing.
Maintenance costs include cleaning, decorating, roof and gutter repair, servicing of the heating system and replacing worn parts, and they recur throughout the life of the house.
Durable, low-maintenance materials such as brick and uPVC windows reduce long-term repair and decoration costs, because they need less upkeep.
Energy-efficient design lowers running costs over the life of the house, even where it adds to the initial cost, so spending more at the start can save money overall.
A cheap build can cost more over time if it has poor insulation, weak materials or a costly heating system, because repairs and heating bills add up.
notes.tip: Marks go to the feature, the reason it saves energy or money, and the link to the family's situation, so say how a choice trades initial cost against running cost.

notes.h: Regulation of house-building standards (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Buildings must be safe, durable and energy efficient, so the State sets legal standards and checks them, and builders can offer warranties. Each method has a name, someone who runs it and a job to do.
points: The Building Regulations are legal standards for the design and construction of buildings, made under the Building Control Act 1990. They cover safety, materials and construction, including structure, fire safety, resistance to moisture, sound, ventilation, hygiene, drainage, heat-producing appliances, stairs and guards, insulation, heating, lighting and waste.
Technical guidance is issued in parts: Part L covers conservation of fuel and energy and Part M covers access and use for people with disabilities.
Local authorities, acting as building control authorities, enforce the Building Regulations through building control and inspect building work.

Under the Building Control (Amendment) Regulations 2014, new building works must be notified to the building control authority with a commencement notice, with certificates of compliance on design, and an assigned certifier and a builder who undertake to inspect and build in line with the regulations.

On completion, a certificate of compliance on completion, signed by the builder and the assigned certifier, is lodged with the building control authority and recorded on a public register before the building is opened or occupied. The aim is to hold designers, builders and certifiers responsible for compliance.
A structural defects warranty such as HomeBond's covers the cost of repairing major structural defects in a new home for ten years from completion.
HomeBond is a company whose registered builders' homes are inspected during construction. Lenders often require such a warranty, or equivalent latent defects insurance, before lending on a new home.

SEAI (Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland) home energy grants support the cost of insulation, heating upgrades such as heat pumps, and solar panels in existing homes, with the aim of improving energy efficiency.
Standards matter for safety, comfort, durability and energy saving, a lender may require them, and they protect resale value.
notes.tip: Name each method (the Building Regulations, a structural defects warranty, the BER), say who runs it and what it does, and say why standards matter. Remember the Building Regulations are made under the Building Control Act 1990, and the certificate of compliance on completion is a different document from the BER.

keyTerms.definition: The design of a space and its fittings to suit how people move, reach and work in it.
The direction a house or room faces, which determines how much daylight and solar heat it receives.
Designing a house's layout, orientation and glazing so that it captures and retains solar heat without mechanical systems.
A Building Energy Rating certificate that rates a home's energy efficiency from A to G.
A certificate confirming that completed building work meets the Building Regulations.
The system through which local authorities enforce the Building Regulations on new building work.
A fault in the structure of a building, such as in its foundations, walls or roof, that affects its stability.
A guarantee, such as HomeBond's, that covers major structural defects in a new home for a set period.
A heating system divided into zones, each with its own thermostat or timer, so that rooms are heated only when needed.
The cost of acquiring the site and building the house, before the home is occupied.

factCards.term: Three factors that influence house design
factCards.definition: Aesthetic and environmental factors; present and future family requirements; initial and maintenance costs.

factCards.term: Four elements a BER assessor measures
factCards.definition: Room and window areas; wall thickness and insulation levels; the heating system; the floor and wall types.

factCards.term: Three points of the kitchen work triangle
factCards.definition: The sink, the cooker and the fridge.

factCards.term: Three areas covered by the Building Regulations
factCards.definition: Safety, materials and construction; insulation, heating and lighting; ventilation and waste.

factCards.term: Two protections given by HomeBond's scheme
factCards.definition: Cover for major structural defects in the home; protection of the buyer's deposit if a registered builder fails.

questions.prompt: State three features of house design that improve energy efficiency and explain how each reduces energy use.
questions.model: Insulation in the roof, walls or cavity reduces heat loss, so less fuel is needed to keep rooms warm. Double glazing reduces heat loss through windows. Zoned heating with thermostats and timers heats only the rooms in use at the times they are needed. Passive solar design, with south-facing glazing, captures solar heat for free. Any three features, each linked to a reduction in heat loss or energy use, earn the marks.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the suitability of a two-storey house with a ground-floor kitchen and living room, three upstairs bedrooms and one bathroom for a family of two adults and three young children, one of whom uses a wheelchair. Suggest two modifications.
questions.model: Suitability for the family: three bedrooms may be adequate for a family of five, but the children may share and need storage. Ground-floor kitchen and living room suit family life. The wheelchair user cannot reach the upstairs bedrooms or the single bathroom, so the layout is unsuitable without changes. Circulation and doors must be wide enough for a wheelchair. Aspect and energy efficiency: the house should be checked for south-facing living space and insulation. Modifications: provide a ground-floor bedroom and an accessible bathroom with level or ramped access and wide doors, or install a stairlift; lower switches and sockets; add a utility room or storage. Any two sensible modifications, justified for this family, earn the marks, and the evaluation should reach a conclusion on suitability.
